title: Rohit and Kohli Will Be at Mullanpur on June 9. The Afghanistan Test Will Still Be Going. The BCCI Is Running Both.
excerpt: India's ODI squad will hold a three-day preparatory camp at the same ground where the one-off Test against Afghanistan may still be in progress. The staff will split. The net bowlers are already drafted. The temperature is forty degrees.
body:
In most countries, a Test match and a white-ball training camp happen in different cities. India is running both at the same ground, at the same time, in forty-degree heat.

The Indian ODI squad — including Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, and Shreyas Iyer — will assemble at the Maharaja Yadavindra Singh International Cricket Stadium in Mullanpur, New Chandigarh, on June 9 for a three-day preparatory camp ahead of the Afghanistan ODI series. The first ODI is on June 13 in Dharamsala. The one-off Test against Afghanistan at the same Mullanpur ground starts on June 6 and could extend until June 10.

The overlap is not accidental. It is a design choice — and one that tells you exactly how seriously the BCCI is taking the 2027 ODI World Cup.

## Two Formats, One Venue, One Staff

The scheduling creates a logistical puzzle that would confuse most boards. The Indian support staff has drawn up a contingency plan: if the Test extends beyond Day 3, coaching and support personnel will split workloads, simultaneously managing the red-ball game while overseeing the white-ball specialists' net sessions at adjacent training facilities.

Sairaj Bahutule, recently appointed as India's spin bowling coach, will be among the staff juggling both groups. The ODI squad includes several players who are not part of the Test side — Rohit, Kohli, Iyer, and the returning Ishan Kishan among them — which at least avoids the problem of players appearing in two squads at once.

But the heat is a variable that cannot be managed with a spreadsheet. Temperatures in Mullanpur have been hovering around 40°C. For players coming off the grinding intensity of a two-month IPL season, the transition to international cricket in that kind of heat is not just demanding — it is medically significant.

## Pacers and the Heat Equation

The BCCI's selection committee has drafted in a specialised group of net bowlers — Gurjapneet Singh, Auqib Nabi, Prince Yadav, Saransh Jain, Zeeshan Ansari, and Shivang Kumar — to ensure the Test match pacers are not asked to bowl full-throttle in nets on top of their match workload.

Mohammed Siraj, Prasidh Krishna, and Gurnoor Brar are the frontline seamers for the Afghanistan Test. Asking them to then bowl at Rohit and Kohli in ODI nets at the same venue, in the same week, in forty-degree heat, would be a recipe for injury. The net bowlers are the buffer that keeps the system from breaking.

## The World Cup Clock Is Ticking

The Mullanpur camp is not just about the three ODIs against Afghanistan. It is about the 2027 Men's ODI World Cup in South Africa, which is now less than a year away. The BCCI is treating every white-ball series between now and then as a rehearsal, and the Afghanistan ODIs — the first since Rohit and Kohli's return to 50-over cricket — are the opening act.

India's ODI squad features a blend of experience and fresh blood: Rohit Sharma as captain, Kohli in the middle order, Ishan Kishan back after a three-year absence, and Prince Yadav earning a first call-up. The camp gives Gambhir's coaching staff three days to align a squad that includes players who have not trained together since the IPL split them across eight franchises.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs tracking Indian cricket from abroad, the next sixty days are the most packed in the sport's history. One Test, six ODIs, and seven T20Is across three countries — Afghanistan at home, Ireland in Belfast, England across five cities — before the calendar finally exhales.

The Mullanpur overlap is a microcosm of Indian cricket's broader reality: there is too much cricket, not enough rest, and a World Cup that waits for no one. The BCCI's solution is not to slow down but to run two programmes in parallel, in the same place, and hope the logistics hold.

If the Test finishes early — and most India-Afghanistan Tests do — the camp will have the ground to itself. If it goes the distance, Mullanpur will briefly become the most crowded cricket facility on the planet: one Test match and one World Cup preparation, separated by a few hundred metres and forty degrees of Punjab summer.
author: Diaspora Desk
